questions.title: How does the Cayley transform guarantee orthogonality in BOFT’s butterfly components?
questions.question_body: In BOFT, each butterfly component $	ilde{ m{B}}^b_{(d,i)}$ is said to be orthogonal by applying a Cayley transform to its $2b	imes2b$ blocks. I understand the Cayley transform for a general skew‑symmetric matrix $ m{Q}$ produces an orthogonal matrix $ m{R}=( m{I}+ m{Q})( m{I}- m{Q})^{-1}$. However, when the component is block‑diagonal with many $2	imes2$ or $2b	imes2b$ sub‑blocks, how does the global orthogonality follow? Are there any subtle constraints on the skew‑symmetric sub‑matrices or on the ordering of parameters that I need to be aware of? Also, does initializing $ m{Q}$ with zeros always give me an identity matrix for each component?

questions.title: Why does BOFT use only $	frac12(b-1)dm$ effective trainable parameters and not $d^2$ as a dense orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BOFT(m,b) requires 	frac12(b-1)dm effective trainable parameters per linear layer. Can someone walk through a concrete example, say with $d=8$, $b=2$, $m=3$, and show exactly how the parameters are counted? I am confused whether every non‑zero entry in each butterfly factor is trainable or if some entries are fixed to $	heta$s or $0$ due to orthogonality constraints. How does this counting change when we vary $b$ or switch from $m$ components to a single full dataset?

questions.title: What is the precise relation between OFT’s block‑diagonal structure and BOFT’s butterfly structure in terms of expressivity?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than OFT for the same block size, but I would like to see a formal argument. Does BOFT contain all block‑diagonal orthogonal matrices as a subset? In particular, can we set particular parameters in BOFT such that $	ilde{ m{B}}^b_{(d,i)}=	ext{diag}( m{B}_i)$ for each level, and would this reduce exactly to OFT’s block‑diagonal case? Conversely, are there orthogonal matrices representable by BOFT that cannot be realized by any block‑diagonal OFT irrespective of block size?

questions.title: How does the information transmission view enforce dense connectivity while keeping edge count minimal?
questions.question_body: The paper describes an information transmission graph over a $(d	imes(m+1))$ grid, where edges correspond to non‑zero entries in the factor matrices. Could someone illustrate how a butterfly factorization achieves *full* connectivity with only O($d	ilde{ f log}d$) edges? What guarantees me that there will be at least one path from every source node (first level) to every sink node (last level)? And why cannot a random sparse pattern with fewer edges produce the same dense connectivity?

questions.title: Is the multiplicative dropout scheme in BOFT equivalent to standard dropout applied after weight multiplication?
questions.question_body: Multiplicative dropout replaces randomly selected butterfly components or diagonal blocks with identity matrices during training. When training proceeds, these components are removed multiplicatively. How does this affect gradient flow compared to standard dropout which zeros out activations or weights additively? What is the mathematical motivation behind choosing identity matrices rather than scaling factors or random signs?

questions.title: Can BOFT handle non‑power‑of‑two dimensionality without changing its factorization scheme?
questions.question_body: BOFT defines butterfly factorizations for dimensions $d=2^N$. In practice many layers have dimension 768 or 1024 which are power of two, but others may not (e.g., 512×4096). If we need to finetune a linear layer where input dimension $d$ is not a power of two, how do we construct a valid butterfly product? Do we pad with zeros/identity rows and columns, or is there an alternative factorization approach? What kind of degradation in performance or parameter count might occur?

questions.title: Why does preserving pairwise angles between neurons lead to better generalization?
questions.question_body: Both OFT and BOFT claim that maintaining pairwise angles between neuron vectors preserves pretraining knowledge and improves generalization. Intuitively I see that an orthogonal transform preserves dot products up to sign. Could someone articulate why this property is more beneficial than simply using small learning rates or L2 regularization? Are there theoretical results linking angle preservation to lower information loss during fine‑tuning?

questions.title: "Spectral norm preservation" and its effect on training stability: could you provide a small derivation?
questions.question_body:
The paper notes that multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserves singular values (and thus spectral norm) of the pretrained weight matrix $ m{W}^0$, which supposedly stabilizes training. Could we show step by step how $
orms{ m{R} m{W}^0}_2 = 
orms{ m{W}^0}_2$ holds when $ m R$ is orthogonal? And how does this imply that gradients remain bounded during backpropagation compared to LoRA where additive updates may change singular values?

questions.title: "Inductive bias via butterfly structures" - what modern theory backs up this claim?
questions.question_body: The authors argue that because butterfly matrices cover classic transforms like FFT, DCT, etc., they impose an implicit bias helpful for generalization. In machine learning theory, we speak about inductive biases in terms of hypothesis classes and VC dimension etc. Is there any research quantifying how much of an inductive bias butterfly parameterization introduces compared with block‐diagonal OFT or LoRA? If not concretely quantified, can we at least intuitively explain how this subspace of $	ext{O}(d)$ yields better regularisation?
